newsitem.title: USA: Maine forest clearcutting ban seen likely to lose.
newsitem.headline: Maine forest clearcutting ban seen likely to lose.

text.p: Voters appeared ready to send a ban on clearcutting in the nation's most heavily wooded state to the chopping block, but an alternative measure may not get enough support to avoid another election.

The battle over logging regulations, pitting three referendum questions against one another, has sparked divisions within the environmental and logging communities and at times has overshadowed Maine's congressional contests.

A recent Strategic Marketing Services poll gave the proposed ban only 16 percent support, compared to 46 percent for a compromise that would tighten restrictions but not stop clearcuts. A measure to keep current logging rules had about 16 percent support.
The winning referendum measure must receive more than 50 percent to avoid being subjected to a second up-or-down vote in a special election without the alternatives.

Maine's environmental Green Party sparked the debate when it stunned political leaders and the powerful paper industry by collecting 58,000 signatures last year to force the referendum on the proposal to ban clearcuts, known as Question 2A on the ballot.

Gov. Angus King persuaded the paper industry to negotiate a compromise with other environmental groups and state legislators placed "The Compact for Maine's Forest" -- Question 2B -- on the ballot, along with a legally required "none of the above" option called Question 2C.

Question 2B's supporters have raised $6.1 million and bombarded the television airwaves with advertisements, many featuring King, who is the nation's only independent governor and very popular with voters.

Supporters of clearcutting, in which all trees are removed from an area, contend the practice is a needed forest management tool and claim the proposed ban would cost 15,000 jobs and destroy Maine's forest-based economy.

Supporters of a complete ban, who have raised $306,000, contend Question 2B, the compact, would allow more clearcutting than current law. They argue that increased use of selective cutting instead of clearcutting would both create jobs and protect timber resources.

Question 2C supporters, primarily owners of small woodlots, contend any new restrictions on clearcutting would have been defeated if King and large landowners had not put the alternative compact on the ballot.
"The governor should be spanked," said Mary Adams, fiesty leader of pro-Question 2C group "Stop the Backroom Deal."

Maine's forests of spruce, fir and hardwood trees have been central to its economy since the first European settlers arrived. Forest-product manufacturing is the state's largest industry, employing 32,000 people.
Nearly 90 percent of Maine's acreage is woodlands. Most of the commercial forest is privately owned and located in the northern half of the state.
